extracted.intended_audience: transportation and environmental professionals, NEPA practitioners, and administrative law counsel interested in agency rulemaking and licensing decisions
extracted.subtask_description: A one-page case-summary of the U.S. Supreme Court decision in Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (435 U.S. 519, 1978), addressing agency procedural discretion in rulemaking and the adequacy of environmental review in licensing. Useful for practitioners assessing when courts may require additional procedures beyond those an agency follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency procedural discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Absent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances the administrative agencies should be free to fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods of inquiry capable of permitting them to discharge their multitudinous duties." (Quoted holding)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court's holding establishes a default principle of judicial deference: agencies generally may determine their own procedural practices for decisionmaking and rulemaking. Courts should not impose extra procedural requirements on agencies except when a constitutional constraint or an exceptionally compelling reason exists. Use this standard when evaluating whether courts may invalidate agency procedures or force additional process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural compliance with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court of appeals found that the AEC "had employed all procedures required by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)," yet nonetheless concluded the rulemaking was insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact pattern highlights two related criteria: (1) whether an agency followed the procedural steps mandated by the APA (notice, opportunity for comment, record), and (2) whether compliance with those steps alone will satisfy judicial review. Vermont Yankee indicates that complying with APA procedures is generally the baseline; courts should be cautious about requiring procedures beyond statutory APA requirements unless a strong justification exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy/substantive sufficiency of rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the AEC followed APA procedures, the court of appeals considered the rulemaking "insufficient" and overturned the rule; the Supreme Court reversed that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing rulemaking adequacy, distinguish procedural compliance from substantive sufficiency. Vermont Yankee supports the view that courts should not substitute their own judgments about an agency's substantive adequacy of inquiry or reasoning unless constitutional or statutory limits are implicated. Evaluate whether the agency's record and reasoned explanation meet the applicable legal standards before concluding a rulemaking is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of environmental impacts (EIS and fuel-cycle analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AEC prepared an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for the licensing request and later conducted a study of the environmental effects associated with the uranium fuel cycle; based on that study the AEC issued a final rule addressing how fuel-cycle impacts should be considered and determined they were insignificant, so it did not reconsider the Vermont Yankee license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating NEPA and licensing decisions, check that (a) an EIS or required NEPA analysis was prepared for the action, (b) subsequent studies or rulemakings that bear on environmental impacts are reasoned and in the administrative record, and (c) the agency explains why any identified impacts are insignificant or do not require reconsideration. Vermont Yankee illustrates that agencies may rely on studies and rulemaking conclusions about environmental significance, and courts should defer to those determinations absent compelling reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of flawed rulemaking on prior agency decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court of appeals overturned the license because the AEC's decision to grant the license was based, in part, on the 'faulty' rulemaking proceeding; the Supreme Court reversed the appeals court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a later-found defect in an agency's rulemaking process invalidates prior actions that relied on that rulemaking. Vermont Yankee signals caution: not every procedural or analytic flaw in a rulemaking will automatically void dependent agency decisions. Determine whether the alleged flaw actually prejudiced the decisionmaker's judgment or violated constitutional/statutory constraints sufficient to warrant reversal.
